[[File:Johann Dryander (11498078).jpg|thumb|right|Johannes Dryander portrait]]
'''Johannes Dryander''', also known as '''Johannes Eichmann''' (1500-1560), was an academic.

==Biography==
Dryander was born in Wetter, [[Holy Roman Empire]] as Johannes Eichmann. He studied [[anatomy]] and [[medicine]] at the [[University of Paris]] and the [[University of Erfurt]] from 1528 to 1534 before becoming a professor of medicine at the [[University of Marburg]] in 1535.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/science/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/johannes-dryander|title=Johannes Dryander}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lib.uiowa.edu/|title=University Libraries &#124; The University of Iowa}}</ref> 

Dryander held two public dissections in the following year and authored the first text illustrating a [[Galenic corpus|Galenic dissection]] of the [[human brain]] in 1536.<ref name="auto">{{Cite journal|title=Dryander of Marburg and the first textbook of neuroanatomy|first1=W. C.|last1=Hanigan|first2=W.|last2=Ragen|first3=R.|last3=Foster|date=March 28, 1990|journal=Neurosurgery|volume=26|issue=3|pages=489–498|doi=10.1097/00006123-199003000-00017|pmid=2181335}}</ref> His ''Anatomiae pars prior'', an expanded edition published in 1537, marked a significant transition from medieval scholasticism to the precise observations of [[Andreas Vesalius]].<ref name="auto"/>

Dryander's books featured detailed illustrations of the brain, skull, and cranial sutures, reflecting his personal use of dissections.<ref name="auto"/> His translation of Mundinus' anatomy in 1542 drew the ire of the anatomist as it plagiarized a portion of Vesalius' ''Tabulae sex''.<ref name="auto"/> He continued his work on [[astrology]] and [[mathematics]] until his death in 1560.<ref name="auto"/> 

His early books, as products of rational scientific thought, contributed significantly to the development of modern anatomy.<ref name="auto"/>
